Belly
BEL-ly
n. (rendering Hebrew beten/me'eh, Greek koilia)
From Saxon baelg, a bag or skin, whence also bellows — the belly is the body's bag. Hebrew beten is the abdomen or womb; me'eh, the inward parts. Greek koilia is a hollow, used of the stomach, the womb, and figuratively of the innermost man.

Biblical Definition

The Authorized Version uses belly where modern speech would say stomach, womb, or the inward man, and Scripture puts it to work in three directions. It is the seat of appetite, and appetite can be enthroned: Paul writes of men “whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things” (Philippians 3:19) — a religion of gratification, and he weeps as he names it. It is the place of confinement in the great sign of the resurrection: “as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40), and Jonah himself prays from a deeper place still: “out of the belly of hell cried I” (Jonah 2:2). And it is the innermost man from which the Spirit's supply overflows to others: “He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38). Set together, these uses are a small anatomy of the heart. The same interior can be a god demanding to be fed, a grave from which a man cries, or a spring from which rivers run; and which it is depends on whether the Holy Ghost has taken possession of it.

Webster 1828 Definition

The part of the body containing the bowels; the womb; and by figure the innermost part of a man. In Scripture, those whose God is their belly, Jonah in the whale's belly and crying from the belly of hell, and the believer out of whose belly flow rivers of living water.

expand to see more

BELLY, n. 1. That part of the human body which extends from the breast to the thighs, containing the bowels.

2. The womb. Jer. 1.

3. The part of anything which resembles the human belly in protuberance or cavity; as, the belly of a flagon.

4. From Saxon baelg, a bag or skin; whence bellows, a bag for wind.

5. In Scripture, whose God is their belly, Phil. 3; out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water, John 7.

Key Scripture

Philippians 3:19 — "Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.)"

Matthew 12:40 — "For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth."

Jonah 2:2 — "And said, I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice."

John 7:38 — "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water."

Modern Corruption

Bodily appetite is treated as morally neutral and therefore ungovernable, so that self-indulgence loses the name of idolatry; and the body itself is either despised as the soul's prison or exalted as the whole of the man.

expand to see more

Paul does not call the men of Philippians 3:19 weak; he calls their belly their god, which makes indulgence a form of worship and not merely a failure of willpower. That category has almost disappeared. Appetite — for food, for drink, for sexual gratification, for comfort, for the endless small consumptions the age arranges to be always available — is now discussed as preference, or as wiring, or at worst as an unhealthy pattern to be managed. Scripture's word is idolatry, and the remedy is correspondingly larger: not technique but repentance, not management but a rival love. The apostle's own answer in the same passage is to set the citizenship in heaven and the coming of the Saviour against the earthly mind, because an appetite is only dethroned by a better object.

The two errors about the body itself flank this. Ancient gnosticism, and the ascetic strain that survived it, treated the flesh as the soul's prison and holiness as escape from it, which Colossians 2:23 answers directly: such severity to the body is of no value against the indulgence of the flesh. The modern error is the opposite, treating the body as the whole of a man and its satisfactions as the sum of his good. Scripture holds the true doctrine between them: the body is the temple of the Holy Ghost, bought with a price, destined for resurrection, and therefore neither to be despised nor obeyed. John 7:38 gives the positive picture — an inward man so filled by the Spirit that what comes out of him is a river for others, which is exactly what a belly-god can never produce.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew beten, the belly or womb; me'eh, the inward parts or bowels; Greek koilia, a hollow, the stomach, the womb, and the inner man.

expand to see more

Hebrew beten (H990) — the belly, and frequently the womb; “before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee” (Jeremiah 1:5).

Hebrew me'eh (H4578) — the inward parts, bowels; the seat of deep feeling in Hebrew idiom (Isaiah 16:11).

Hebrew mē'āh in Jonah 2:1 — the fish's inward parts, from which the prophet's psalm is prayed.

Greek koilia (G2836) — a hollow; the belly, the womb, and by figure the innermost being (John 7:38).

Greek gastēr (G1064) — the stomach or womb; whence gastrimargia, gluttony, in later Greek moral writing.

Usage

"Of appetite enthroned as a god: whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame (Philippians 3:19)."

"Of the sign of the prophet Jonas: as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly (Matthew 12:40)."

"Of the Spirit's overflow in a believer: out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water (John 7:38)."
